title: Ezekiel 23:22–35
context: The Lord GOD now addresses Oholibah (Jerusalem) through the prophet, announcing that he will raise up the Babylonians, the Chaldeans, and others against her, so that the nations she relied on become the instruments of her judgment, and that she will drink her sister Samaria’s cup, “the cup of astonishment and desolation.” The judgment imagery is violent and is described here only in general terms; it is prophetic allegory about the nation’s fall to Babylon, not a pattern for how any person should be treated, and readers in both traditions acknowledge that it is hard to read. Both traditions share the ground that the LORD judges covenant unfaithfulness justly, the cup recalls Jeremiah 25:15, and the question of how God uses the nations points to the existing box at Judges 9:23 rather than a new one.

verses.text: “Therefore, Oholibah, the Lord GOD says: ‘Behold, I will raise up your lovers against you, from whom your soul is alienated, and I will bring them against you on every side:
verses.arminianNotes:
The Lord GOD says to Oholibah, “Behold, I will raise up your lovers against you.” Arminian readers note that “the Lord GOD” renders Adonai joined to the divine name.

The nations Jerusalem relied on will turn against her.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see judgment arising from the very powers trusted in place of God.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that misplaced trust becomes the means of judgment.

verses.text: the Babylonians and all the Chaldeans, Pekod, Shoa, Koa, and all the Assyrians with them; all of them desirable young men, governors and rulers, princes and men of renown, all of them riding on horses.
verses.arminianNotes:
The attackers include “the Babylonians and all the Chaldeans, Pekod, Shoa, Koa, and all the Assyrians with them.” Arminian readers note the coalition of peoples.

Pekod, Shoa, and Koa are not securely identified.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise hold the identifications lightly.

Shared ground: both traditions read the list as the forces under Babylon’s command, and both note that the same description of Assyrian and Babylonian splendor from earlier in the chapter now names Jerusalem’s attackers.

verses.text: They will come against you with weapons, chariots, and wagons, and with a company of peoples. They will set themselves against you with buckler, shield, and helmet all around. I will commit the judgment to them, and they will judge you according to their judgments.
verses.arminianNotes:
“They will come against you with weapons, chariots, and wagons.” The LORD says, “I will commit the judgment to them.” Arminian readers note that the LORD hands judgment over to the Babylonian army.

The nations act according to their own ways.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God governing the nations as instruments of judgment.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that God remains just while using human armies.

verses.text: I will set my jealousy against you, and they will deal with you in fury. They will take away your nose and your ears. Your remnant will fall by the sword. They will take your sons and your daughters; and the rest of you will be devoured by the fire.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says, “I will set my jealousy against you,” and describes the invaders’ fury in violent images of the city’s fall. Arminian readers read these as allegory of Jerusalem’s destruction.

They describe the details only in general terms.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise read the verse soberly as judgment on the nation, not as an endorsement of violence against any person.

Shared ground: both traditions acknowledge, with care, that readers find this imagery hard, and both read the LORD’s jealousy as covenant love wounded by betrayal.

verses.text: They will also strip you of your clothes and take away your beautiful jewels.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says the invaders will “take away your beautiful jewels.” Arminian readers note that the city’s wealth and adornment will be taken.

The image pictures Jerusalem emptied of its glory.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the loss of everything Jerusalem had gained or trusted in.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as allegory of the city’s plundering, described soberly and without expansion.

verses.text: Thus I will make your lewdness to cease from you, and remove your prostitution from the land of Egypt, so that you will not lift up your eyes to them, nor remember Egypt any more.’
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says the judgment will end Jerusalem’s unfaithfulness, “so that you will not lift up your eyes to them, nor remember Egypt any more.” Arminian readers note the purpose of ending the pattern.

Judgment is aimed at stopping the long sin.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see judgment as purging the nation’s idolatry.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that the LORD’s purpose includes ending the reliance on Egypt that had marked Judah’s history.

verses.text: “For the Lord GOD says: ‘Behold, I will deliver you into the hand of them whom you hate, into the hand of them from whom your soul is alienated.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Lord GOD says, “Behold, I will deliver you into the hand of them whom you hate.” Arminian readers note the bitter reversal: Jerusalem is handed over to those she has come to despise.

The theme of 23:17 returns.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God’s judgment through the nations Jerusalem had turned from.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the consequence of shifting alliances, and agree that God is just in it.

verses.text: They will deal with you in hatred, and will take away all your labor, and will leave you naked and bare. The nakedness of your prostitution will be uncovered, both your lewdness and your prostitution.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says the invaders “will take away all your labor,” and the chapter’s strong imagery of exposure returns. Arminian readers note that Jerusalem loses all it has worked for.

The details are described here only in general terms.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise read the verse as the shame of a city laid bare by conquest.

Shared ground: both traditions read the imagery soberly as allegory of national humiliation and loss.

verses.text: These things will be done to you because you have played the prostitute after the nations, and because you are polluted with their idols.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD explains that these things come “because you are polluted with their idols.” Arminian readers note that the judgment is grounded in idolatry.

The allegory’s meaning is stated directly here.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see idolatry named as the root of the nation’s guilt.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that the chapter’s imagery serves to expose covenant unfaithfulness and idolatry, which is its plain point.

verses.text: You have walked in the way of your sister; therefore I will give her cup into your hand.’
verses.arminianNotes:
“You have walked in the way of your sister; therefore I will give her cup into your hand.” Arminian readers note the cup image, which also appears in Jeremiah 25:15.

Jerusalem will share Samaria’s judgment.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise read the cup as an image of God’s righteous judgment.

Shared ground: both traditions point to the notes on Jeremiah 25:15 rather than adding a new discussion, and agree that the sisters’ shared path leads to a shared cup.

verses.text: “The Lord GOD says: ‘You will drink of your sister’s cup, which is deep and large. You will be ridiculed and held in derision. It contains much.
verses.arminianNotes:
“You will drink of your sister’s cup, which is deep and large. You will be ridiculed and held in derision.” Arminian readers note the depth of the judgment.

Shame accompanies the loss.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the cup as full and certain.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as poetic language for Jerusalem’s fall, consistent with the cup imagery in Jeremiah 25.

verses.text: You will be filled with drunkenness and sorrow, with the cup of astonishment and desolation, with the cup of your sister Samaria.
verses.arminianNotes:
“You will be filled with drunkenness and sorrow, with the cup of astonishment and desolation, with the cup of your sister Samaria.” Arminian readers note the grief in the image.

The cup brings sorrow, not only punishment.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the desolation that follows unfaithfulness.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse with sorrow and note that it names Samaria directly, tying the two sisters’ fates together.

verses.text: You will even drink it and drain it out. You will gnaw the broken pieces of it, and will tear your breasts; for I have spoken it,’ says the Lord GOD.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says Jerusalem will drink the cup to its end, ending with “for I have spoken it,” says the Lord GOD. Arminian readers note the certainty of the word.

The imagery of anguish is described here only in general terms.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the finality of God’s spoken judgment.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse soberly as a picture of complete anguish in the city’s fall, without repeating its imagery.

verses.text: “Therefore the Lord GOD says: ‘Because you have forgotten me and cast me behind your back, therefore you also bear your lewdness and your prostitution.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
“Because you have forgotten me and cast me behind your back.” Arminian readers note that the root sin is forgetting the LORD.

The rest of the verse sums up the consequences of that forgetting.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the heart of the indictment in the turning away from God himself.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that the whole allegory comes down to this: the people forgot the LORD who had made them his own (23:4).
